content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp gumbo is a classic Creole stew from Louisiana, first recorded in 1915. It is a thick, roux‑based soup with onions, celery, bell pepper, a blend of spices, and large shrimp. Served over rice, gumbo offers a rich, slightly spicy flavor with hints of hot sauce and aromatic herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word "gumbo" comes from the African term "kiMbi," meaning "soup".
1915 is considered the official year of the first published shrimp gumbo recipe in American culinary magazines.
Traditional gumbo uses a dark roux—cooked flour—that gives the dish its characteristic color and thickness.
Large North Atlantic shrimp are typically used, retaining a delicate taste even after long simmering.
Gumbo is often prepared in huge kettles over open fire during New Orleans festivals.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide a high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat stews, shrimp gumbo contains little saturated fat.

items.title: Source of iodine and selenium
items.content: Seafood is rich in iodine and selenium, supporting thyroid function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp contain vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Thyme, bay leaf, and paprika used in gumbo have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Gumbo often includes broth and soy sauce, raising the salt level.

items.title: Portion size
items.content: The dish is typically served in large bowls, so watch the amount of accompanying rice.

items.title: Mercury concerns
items.content: While shrimp are generally low in mercury, choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gumbo hot over a bed of steamed white rice. Garnish with chopped green onions, parsley, or a squeeze of lemon for brightness. Leftovers keep well in the fridge and can be reheated gently on the stove.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the gumbo to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving to ensure safety.
